content.title: LIFTOFF: Artemis II takes off from Kennedy Space Center
content.text: KENNEDY SPACE CENTER — More than 50 years have passed since humans visited the moon, and history was made on Wednesday as NASA launched its crewed Artemis II for a flyby of Earth’s lunar sister. What You Need To Know Artemis II to return humans to the moon in a flyby mission The launch happened Wednesday from Kennedy Space Center A few things made the launch a bit iffy, such as an issue with the Space Launch System rocket's flight-termination system; but the launch was successful Get more space coverage here ▶ RELATED coverage: NASA says Artemis II launch is still on target; explains moon base NASA repairs helium flow issue that caused Artemis II rollback NASA: Artemis III will not land on the moon Looking back at Artemis I as NASA makes final preps for Artemis II mission Get the full Artemis II coverage here ▶ 🔻Scroll down to see the Artemis II mission breakdown🔻 🔻Scroll down to meet the Artemis II crew🔻 Artemis II's Cmdr. Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency mission specialist Jeremy Hansen climbed into the Orion capsule, which was on top of the Space Launch System rocket, and left Earth from Launch Pad 39B at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 6:35 p.m. ET. The rocket roared like a powerful lion as it raced into the blue sky, as spectators and space lovers hailed it and the crew on as if their cheers were additional fuel. A few things made the launch a bit iffy, such as an issue with the Space Launch System rocket's flight-termination system. An unspecified issue happened with the rocket’s flight-termination system, which would send a self-destruct signal to the rocket in case it veered off course and was heading to a populated area. But NASA stated at around 5:15 p.m. ET that the issue had been resolved. "A confidence test was performed to ensure that the hardware is ready to support today’s launch," NASA stated. Another issue that came up before the takeoff was the launch abort system’s attitude control motor controller battery was overheating and NASA technicians were working on a workaround. Evenutally, NASA stated it was OK. "Engineers investigated a sensor on the launch abort system’s attitude control motor controller battery that showed a higher temperature than would be expected. It is believed to be an instrumentation issue and will not affect today’s launch," NASA stated. Wednesday morning started off well, as NASA was able to fuel the gigantic Space Launch System rocket. Shortly after noon, NASA said the liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen fast fill were complete for the Space Launch System upper stage. This was an impressive feat as a liquid hydrogen leak caused the launch to be pushed back. Scroll down to understand the history. A little after 2 p.m. ET, the foursome were seen heading for their ride to the moon. The Space Launch System rocket is massive. It is a 322-foot (98.27-meter) tall super-heavy rocket that is 17 feet (5.18 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty. For all of you space lovers out there, this graphic puts its height in perspective. Spectrum News meteorologist Zach Covey gave updates on the weather days leading up to the launch. The forecast jumped from being 80% favorable just days away from the liftoff to 90% on the launch day. Rain was threatening the area, but not a drop was felt at the launch pad on Wednesday. In fact, on launch day, Covey explained the importance of the weather. Many people came out to witness the launch themselves and provide insight into the mission. One of them was U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, who as a retired NASA astronaut had a long career on the space shuttle missions and the International Space Station. Former NASA Administrator and retired astronaut Charles Bolden spoke about the importance of the mission. And he was asked if he wanted to join the mission. Understanding the Artemis II mission It will be the first time in more than 50 years that humans have visited Earth’s sister. The 322-foot (98.27-meter) tall moon rocket will take the quartet on a 10-day mission to fly by our planet’s lunar neighbor. The four will be the first humans to visit the moon since the 1972 Apollo 17 mission, which was the last time humans stepped foot on the lunar satellite. And it will be the first test of the Orion capsule, called Integrity, to have humans in it with this first crewed flight of the spacecraft. Since their announcement as the Artemis II crew in 2023, Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen have spent countless hours doing various training, including in a simulator of the capsule. They will also be conducting various experiments, such as how the human body is impacted in a deep spaceflight, a monitoring device that will record participating astronauts’ well-being, activity and sleep patterns, and monitoring radiation levels inside and outside of Orion. Other experiments include looking at blood and saliva samples taken before and after the mission to see how deep space changes the immune system. And the four will not be the only four going up. Four small satellites will hitch a ride and will go into high Earth orbit. Those satellites are from: Argentina National Space Activities Commissions Korea AeroSpace Administration Saudi Space Agency German Aerospace Center Mission Specs: Space Launch System rocket: 322 feet tall Orion: 10 feet, 11 inches tall and 16.5 feet in diameter Mission Duration: 10 days Distance from lunar surface: 4,000 to 6,000 miles Orion's speed once it returns to Earth: 25,000 mph Temps on Orion's heat shield: 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit For the 10-day Artemis II mission, the quartet will only do a flyby of the moon, rather than an orbit. But it will make Glover the first person of color and Koch the first woman to visit the moon. And Hansen will be the first Canadian to visit the lunar satellite. In fact, it is his first time being in space. Hear their thoughts on what being the first means to them On day six of the mission, the four will set a record as the first humans to travel farther than anyone has from Earth. But that distance has not happened yet. The current record was set by the Apollo 13 mission in 1970 with a distance of 248,655 miles (400,171 kilometers) from Earth. If the launch happens on Wednesday, April 01, the new record will be about 252,799 miles (406,841 kilometers) from Earth. During the little trip, the crew will be closest to the moon when they travel to its far side, which is sometimes called the dark side of the moon. Depending on when Artemis II launches, the crew could be between 4,000 to 6,000 miles (6,437 to 9,656 kilometers) from the moon’s surface. NASA described the crew’s view as, “The Artemis II crew will travel approximately 4,600 miles beyond the far side of the moon. They will see the Earth and the moon from Orion’s windows, with the moon close in the foreground and the Earth nearly 250,000 miles in the background. From the crew’s location, the moon will look about the size of a basketball held at arm’s length.” And according to NASA, during this time period, the crew will lose communication with Earth between 30 to 50 minutes. Breakdown of the 10-day mission History of the Artemis II The U.S. has attempted to return to the moon a number of times, like the Constellation program. In 2004, then-President George W. Bush wanted NASA to develop a plan to return humans to the moon once the International Space Station was completely finished and the retirement of the space shuttle in 2010. However, a few years later, then-President Barack Obama cancelled the Constellation program due to it being over budget and behind schedule. The Space Launch System rocket was announced back in 2011, with the goal of returning humans to the moon. During his first term, President Donald Trump pushed for humans to return to the moon, with the name Artemis chosen for the new program. Originally called Exploration Mission-2, the Artemis II mission was expected to launch in 2019, but it was pushed back to 2021. Artemis II was scheduled for launch in November 2024 and then in September 2025, but it was pushed back due to concerns about the heat shield from the uncrewed Artemis I launch in 2022. The main contractors for the SLS are: Boeing: The core stage Northrop Grumman: Space Launch System twin rocket boosters Aerojet Rocketdyne: The four RS-25 engines The main contractors for the Orion capsule: Lockheed Martin European Space Agency During that test flight mission, the Orion capsule’s heat shield performed in different ways and was shedding in ways that were not expected during its re-entry back to Earth. A material called Avcoat that was on the heat shield broke off in lumps during the re-entry phase of Artemis I. The Avcoat material is designed to protect a spacecraft from extreme temperatures by burning away as it heats up, instead of sending that heat to the capsule itself. However, during re-entry, it broke into chunks instead of burning away, stated NASA officials. NASA stated that its experts from various fields determined the root cause of the failure of the heat shield and have come up with a new method to create a better one. The Artemis II was supposed to launch earlier in 2026, but two liquid hydrogen leaks and a helium flow issue pushed it back. Check out the timeline to learn more. Meeting the crew
